source_text:
ὁ δὲ ἀρτίως καὶ τὴν ψυχὴν καὶ τὸ σῶμα ἰατρευθεὶς παρὰ τῆς σοφίας σοφὸν λαβὼν λόγον εὐθὺς
ἀποκρίνεται, οὐ νομικῶς ἀποκριθῆναι ἔχον, ἀλλὰ συντόμως ποιούμενος τὴν ἀπόκρισιν. Ἴστε μου, φησί, πάντες τὴν πολυχρόνιον νόσον καὶ τὸ πολυετὲς τῆς ἀνακλίσεως, τὸ ἀπερίστατον τῆς ταλαιπωρίας. οὐδεὶς ὑμῶν ποτε κηδεμονικὸν ἔδειξεν λαβών με καὶ πρῶτον ἐμβαλὼν εἰς τὴν κολυμβήθραν, ἵνα θεραπευθῶ. καίτοι τότε κηδεμονικὸν οὐκ ἐνδειξάμενοι πῶς νῦν τὸ νομοθετικὸν ἐλάβετε, οὐκ ἔξεστίν σοι ἆραι τὸν κράββατόν σου, λέγοντες; Συντομωτάτην τοίνυν ποιοῦμαι πρὸς ὑμᾶς τὴν ἀπόκρισιν· ὁ ποιήσας με ὑγιῆ ἐκεῖνός μοι εἶπεν. εἰ ἐμοῦ καταφρονεῖτε, πρὸς τὸ πρᾶγμα τὴν ἔκπληξιν λάβετε. οὐκ ἔμπλαστρον ἐπέθηκεν, οὐκ ἰατρικοῖς ἐχρήσατο μηχανήμασιν ἢ βοηθήμασιν. λόγῳ εἶπεν, καὶ τὸ ἔργον ἐπηκολούθησεν. προσέταξε, καὶ τὸ πρόσταγμα ἐγὼ ἐπιτελῶ. εὐπειθὴς γέγονα τούτου τῷ προσ τάγματι τοῦ διὰ προσταγμάτων θεραπεύσαντος. εἰ μὲν γὰρ ὁ προστάξας πρὸς τὸ ἰαθῆναι ἀνίσχυρος ἦν τοῖς προστάγμασιν, οὐκ ἔδει τούτοις ὑπακούειν. ἐπειδὴ δὲ λόγοις προστέτακται ἐναργὲς πολυχρόνιον παῦσαι πάθημα, δικαιότατα ἀκούω τούτου, οὗ καὶ νόσος ἀκούσασα ἀπηλλάγη. ὁ ποιήσας με ὑγιῆ ἐκεῖνός μοι εἶπεν, ἆρον τὸν κράββατόν σου. 16 Οὐκ ᾔδει ὁ θεραπευθείς, τίς ἐστιν ὁ θεραπεύων. πολὺ τὸ ἀκενόδοξον τοῦ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν παρίσταται. ἰατρεύσας γὰρ ἐξέκλινεν, ἵνα μὴ γνωρισθῇ ἐπὶ τῇ ἰατρείᾳ. ἡμεῖς δὲ πᾶν τοὐναντίον ποιοῦμεν. εἰ συμβῇ ποτε ὀνείρατα θεάσασθαι, ἢ διὰ χειρῶν βοηθῆσαι, ἢ δαίμονα δι' ἐπικλήσεως ἀπελάσαι, τοσοῦτον ἀπέχομεν τοῦ κρύψαι τὸ κατόρθωμα, ὥστε καὶ μὴ ἐρωτώμενοι καυχώμεθα. Ἰησοῦς δέ, τοῖς ἔργοις διδάσκων ἡμᾶς τὸ μὴ περὶ ἑαυτοῦ λέγειν, τὴν ἴασιν παρέχων ἐξέκλινεν ἅμα, ἵνα μὴ γνωρίζηται, εὐκαίρως ἀναχωρῶν καὶ εὐκαίρως παρών. ὅτε μὲν γὰρ ἐχρῆν κλεϊσθῆναι τὴν εὐφημίαν τοῦ κατορθώματος, τότε ἀναχωρεῖ. ὅτε δὲ τῶν ὄχλων ἀναχώρησις γέγονεν, ἵνα μετὰ τῆς σωματικῆς ἰατρείας ἐπαγάγῃ καὶ τὰ τῆς ψυχῆς τεθεραπευμένα, τότε παρὼν ἔλεγεν· ἴδε ὑγιὴς γέγονας, μηκέτι ἁμάρτανε. 17 Ποικίλος δέ ἐστιν ἰατρός, ποτὲ μὲν πρῶτον ψυχὴν θεραπεύων, εἶτα σῶμα, ποτὲ δὲ ἀντιστρόφως. μηκέτι ἁμάρτανε, ἵνα μὴ χεῖρόν σοί τι γένηται. διδάσκων δι' ἑνὸς πολλούς. οὐ γὰρ πρὸς ἐκεῖνον μὲν ὁ λόγος μόνον, ἀλλὰ γὰρ καὶ πρὸς πάντας ἡμᾶς. εἴ ποτε γὰρ παθήμασιν περιπέσωμεν ἢ λύπαις ἢ ἀνάγκαις, μηδεὶς θεῷ προσγραφέτω. ὁ γὰρ θεὸς ἀπείραστός ἐστι κακῶν, πειράζει δὲ αὐτὸς οὐδένα. ἕκαστος δὲ ἡμῶν σειραῖς ἁμαρτιῶν σφιγγόμενος μαστιγοῦται. Μηκέτι ἁμάρτανε ἵνα μὴ χεῖρόν σοί τι γένηται. ἄκουε τοῦ ῥητοῦ πᾶς ἄνθρωπος, καὶ ὁ πρὸ τούτου πορνεύων ἀποτιθέσθω τὸ πάθος, καὶ ὁ πρὸ τούτου πλεονέκτης γενοῦ ἐλεήμων. ἀκουέτω ὁ ἅρπαξ, μηκέτι ἁμάρτανε. Πολλὴ καὶ θεοῦ ἡ ἀμνησικακία, δαψιλὴς ἡ χάρις. ἀλλὰ μὴ τὸ ὑπέρμετρον τῆς ἀνεξικακίας ἐφόδιον λάμβανε τῆς καταφρονήσεως, μηδ' ὅτι θεὸς μακρόθυμος, διὰ τοῦτο ἁμάρτανε. ἀλλὰ θεραπεύθητι λοιπὸν τὰ σαρκικὰ πάθη, καὶ λέγε καὶ σὺ τὸ εὐκαίρως ἀναγνωσθέν. ὅτε γὰρ ἦμεν ἐν τῇ σαρκί, τὰ παθήματα τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν τὰ διὰ τοῦ νόμου ἐνηργεῖτο ἐν τοῖς μέλεσιν ἡμῶν ἐὰν δὲ λέγῃ ὁ ἀπόστολος, ὅτε ἦμεν ἐν τῇ σαρκί, οὐ ταύτην ἔλεγεν τὴν σάρκα, ἣν περιβεβλήμεθα, ἀλλὰ τὰς σαρκικὰς πράξεις. ἔτι γε σάρκα φορῶν ἔλεγεν, ὅτε ἦμεν ἐν τῇ σαρκί. ἀλλ' ὅνπερ τρόπον μέλλοντος ἐπάγεσθαι κατακλυσμοῦ ὁ θεὸς ἔλεγεν, οὐ μὴ καταμείνῃ τὸ πνεῦμά μου ἐν τοῖς ἀνθρώποις τούτοις, διὰ τὸ εἶναι αὐτοὺς σάρκας, τοῦ πνεύματος εἰς σαρκικὴν προαίρεσιν μεταβαλλομένου, οὕτως καὶ ἐνταῦθα ὁ ἀπόστολος λέγει, ὅτε ἦμεν ἐν τῇ σαρκί. 18 Μηδεὶς τοίνυν ἔστω ἐν σαρκί, ἀλλ' ἐν σαρκὶ ὢν μὴ κατὰ σάρκα περιπατείτω. οὐ γὰρ βούλεται ἡμᾶς ὁ ἀπόστολος τελείως ἑαυτοὺς ἐξαγαγόντας ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου μὴ ἐργάζεσθαι φαῦλον, ἀλλ' ἐν σαρκὶ ὄντας ἡμᾶς καταδουλῶσαι τὴν σάρκα, καὶ μὴ ἄρχεσθαι ὑπ' αὐτῆς. μὴ δουλωθῶμεν, ἀλλ' ἄρξωμεν. τροφῇ χρησώμεθα συμμέτρῳ, μὴ τῇ γαστριμαργίᾳ καταφερόμενοι, ἀλλὰ χαλινοῦντες τὴν γαστέρα, ἵνα καὶ τῶν ὑπὸ γαστέρα ἄρξωμεν. ἀρχέσθω τὸ σῶμα ὑπὸ τῆς ψυχῆς, καὶ μὴ συρέσθω ἡ ψυχὴ ὑπὸ τῶν σαρκικῶν ἡδονῶν. Μηκέτι ἁμάρτανε, ἵνα μή τί σοι χεῖρον γένηται. κηρύσσει μὲν ἅπασιν ὁ λόγος, γένοιτο δὲ πάντα τὰ ὦτα ἀκούειν. οὐ γὰρ πᾶσα ἀκοὴ σαρκὸς δεχομένη τὸν λόγον ἤδη δέχεται εἰς τὴν διάνοιαν. διὰ τοῦτο ὁ σωτὴρ ἔλεγεν· ὁ ἔχων ὦτα ἀκούειν ἀκουέτω, τοῖς ἔχουσιν ὦτα σαρκὸς διαλεγόμενος. 19 Ἀκουέτω τοίνυν ἅπας Ἰησοῦ καὶ μηκέτι ἁμαρτανέτω, ἀλλὰ τῷ ἁρματιῶν συγχωρητῇ προσδράμωμεν.
thought_title: The healed man's defense and the call to sin no more
orientation: The healed man, given a wise reply by Wisdom, answers the Jews who object to his carrying the mat on the Sabbath, and Cyril then applies Jesus' command 'sin no more' to all hearers.
pass_a_gloss: But the one just now healed in both soul and body, having received from Wisdom a wise word, immediately answers, not having to answer in a legal manner, but making the answer concisely. You all know, he says, my long-lasting disease and the many years of lying down, the unrelieved state of my misery. None of you ever showed a caring act by taking me and first putting me into the pool, so that I might be healed. And yet, having shown no caring act then, how have you now taken up the lawgiving role, saying, It is not lawful for you to take up your mat? I make, then, a very concise answer to you: the one who made me well, that one said to me. If you despise me, take your astonishment at the deed. He did not apply a plaster, he did not use medical devices or remedies. By a word he spoke, and the deed followed. He commanded, and I am carrying out the command. I have become obedient to the command of this one who healed through commands. For if the one who commanded had been powerless in his commands to bring about the healing, it would not have been necessary to obey them. But since by words it has been commanded to stop a clear long-lasting suffering, most justly I obey this one, whom even the disease obeyed and departed. The one who made me well, that one said to me, Take up your mat. 16 The one who was healed did not know who the one healing is. The great freedom from vainglory of our Savior is displayed. For having healed, he withdrew, so that he might not be recognized for the healing. But we do entirely the opposite. If it ever happens that we see dreams, or help with our hands, or drive out a demon by invocation, we are so far from hiding the success that even when not asked we boast. But Jesus, teaching us by his deeds not to speak about oneself, while providing the healing withdrew at the same time, so that he might not be recognized, withdrawing at the right time and being present at the right time. For when it was necessary for the praise of the success to be shut up, then he withdraws. But when the withdrawal of the crowds had happened, so that along with the bodily healing he might bring in also the things of the soul that had been healed, then being present he said: See, you have become well; sin no more. 17 But the physician is varied, sometimes first healing the soul, then the body, sometimes in reverse. Sin no more, so that nothing worse may happen to you. Teaching many through one. For the word is not only to that man, but indeed also to all of us. For if ever we fall into sufferings or griefs or necessities, let no one attribute it to God. For God is untempted by evils, and he himself tempts no one. But each of us, being bound by cords of sins, is scourged. Sin no more, so that nothing worse may happen to you. Let every person hear the saying, and let the one who was fornicating before this put away the passion, and let the one who was greedy before this become merciful. Let the robber hear: sin no more. Great also is God's forgetfulness of wrongs, abundant is the grace. But do not take the excess of his forbearance as provision for contempt, nor because God is long-suffering, for this reason sin. But be healed henceforth of the fleshly passions, and say also you the thing read at the right time. For when we were in the flesh, the passions of sins which were through the law were at work in our members. But if the apostle says, when we were in the flesh, he was not speaking of this flesh which we have put on, but of the fleshly deeds. Still wearing flesh he said, when we were in the flesh. But in the same way that, when a flood was about to be brought on, God said, My spirit shall not remain in these humans, because they are flesh, the spirit being changed into fleshly choice, so also here the apostle says, when we were in the flesh. 18 Let no one, then, be in the flesh, but being in flesh let him not walk according to flesh. For the apostle does not wish that we, having completely removed ourselves from the world, should not do evil, but that being in flesh we enslave the flesh, and not be ruled by it. Let us not be enslaved, but let us rule. Let us use moderate food, not being carried down by gluttony, but bridling the belly, so that we may also rule the things under the belly. Let the body be ruled by the soul, and let not the soul be dragged by fleshly pleasures. Sin no more, so that nothing worse may happen to you. The word proclaims to all, and may it happen that all ears hear. For not every hearing of flesh that receives the word already receives it into the mind. For this reason the Savior said: Let the one who has ears to hear hear, speaking to those who have ears of flesh. 19 Let everyone, then, hear Jesus and sin no more, but let us run to the forgiving one of sins.

choices.term: ἀρτίως καὶ τὴν ψυχὴν καὶ τὸ σῶμα ἰατρευθείς
choices.english: the one just now healed in both soul and body
choices.why: Keeps the adverb 'just now' and the paired objects 'soul and body' in source order, preserving the emphasis on the completeness of the healing.
rejected: the man who had just been healed in soul and body
the recently healed man in both soul and body

choices.why: Renders the substantivized adjective as a noun phrase, preserving the contrast with 'lawgiving role' (νομοθετικόν) later in the same sentence.
Captures the alpha-privative noun as a positive quality of Christ, matching Cyril's rhetorical contrast with human boasting.
Renders the compound literally, preserving the theological nuance of God not remembering wrongs rather than merely forgiving.
Uses the fixed glossary rendering for this key command of Jesus, applied throughout the section.
Uses 'fleshly' for the adjective to distinguish σαρκικός from the noun σάρξ ('flesh'), preserving Cyril's distinction between the physical body and sinful deeds.

pass_b_english: The man who had just now been healed in both soul and body received a wise word from Wisdom, and he answers at once. He does not answer in a legalistic way, but makes his reply brief. "You all know," he says, "my long-lasting illness and my many years of lying down, the helplessness of my misery. Not one of you ever showed a caring act by taking me and putting me first into the pool so that I might be healed. And yet, when you showed no caring act then, how have you now taken up the lawgiving role, saying, 'It is not lawful for you to carry your mat'? I make my answer to you very brief: the one who made me well is the one who told me. If you despise me, let the deed itself amaze you. He applied no plaster; he used no medical devices or remedies. He spoke a word, and the work followed. He commanded, and I am carrying out the command. I have become obedient to the command of the one who healed me by commands. For if the one who commanded had been powerless in his commands to bring about the healing, there would have been no need to obey them. But since by words he commanded a long-lasting affliction to cease, and it clearly did, I am most justly obedient to the one whose command even the illness heard and departed. The one who made me well is the one who told me, 'Take up your mat.'"

The healed man did not know who the healer was. Here the humility of our Savior is on full display. For after healing him, Jesus slipped away so that he would not be recognized for the healing. But we do exactly the opposite. If we ever happen to see visions, or help with our hands, or drive out a demon by invocation, we are so far from hiding the success that we boast even when no one asks. But Jesus, teaching us by his deeds not to speak about ourselves, granted the healing and at the same time slipped away so that he would not be recognized, withdrawing at the right time and being present at the right time. For when the praise of the success needed to be kept quiet, then he withdraws. But when the crowds had dispersed, so that along with the bodily healing he might also bring healing to the soul, then he was present and said: "See, you have become well; sin no more."

He is a varied physician: sometimes he heals the soul first and then the body, and sometimes the reverse. "Sin no more, so that nothing worse happens to you." Through one man he teaches many. For the word was not spoken to that man alone, but to all of us as well. For if we ever fall into afflictions or sorrows or hardships, let no one blame God. For God cannot be tempted by evils, and he himself tempts no one. Each of us is scourged when he is bound fast by the cords of his own sins. "Sin no more, so that nothing worse happens to you." Let every person hear this saying: the one who was committing fornication before, let him put away the passion; the one who was greedy before, become merciful. Let the robber hear: sin no more. Great is God's willingness to forgive wrongs, and abundant is his grace. But do not take the excess of his forbearance as a provision for contempt, and do not sin just because God is patient. Rather, be healed now of the fleshly passions, and say for yourself the words read at the right moment: "For when we were in the flesh, the sinful passions were at work in our members." But when the apostle says "when we were in the flesh," he does not mean this flesh that we are clothed in, but fleshly deeds. He was still wearing flesh when he said, "when we were in the flesh." But just as when the flood was about to be brought on, God said, "My spirit shall not remain in these people, because they are flesh," the spirit being changed into a fleshly choice, so also here the apostle says, "when we were in the flesh."

Let no one, then, be in the flesh; but while being in the flesh, let him not walk according to the flesh. For the apostle does not want us to take ourselves completely out of the world and do no evil; rather, while we are in the flesh, he wants us to enslave the flesh and not be ruled by it. Let us not be enslaved; let us rule. Let us use food in due measure, not being carried away by gluttony, but bridling the stomach so that we may also rule over the desires below it. Let the body be ruled by the soul, and let the soul not be dragged away by fleshly pleasures. "Sin no more, so that nothing worse happens to you." The word proclaims this to all, and may all ears hear it. For not every hearing of the flesh that receives the word already receives it into the mind. That is why the Savior said: "Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear," speaking to those who have ears of flesh.
Let everyone, then, hear Jesus and sin no more, but let us run to the charioteer who grants pardon.

problems.quote: The man who had just now been healed in both soul and body received a wise answer from wisdom and replies at once
problems.source_quote: ὁ δὲ ἀρτίως ... σοφὸν λαβὼν λόγον εὐθὺς ἀποκρίνεται
problems.why: Greek says he, having taken a wise word, replies; English makes him receive an answer from wisdom, reversing agency.
problems.fix: The man who had just now been healed in both soul and body, having taken a wise word, replies at once
problems.ruling: σοφὸν λαβὼν λόγον = 'having received a wise word'; he speaks it, not receives an answer from wisdom. Agency reversed.

edits.old: The man who had just now been healed in both soul and body received a wise answer from wisdom and replies at once
edits.new: The man who had just now been healed in both soul and body, having taken a wise word, replies at once

fixed: Agency: source says he, having taken a wise word, replies; English reversed agency by making him receive an answer from wisdom. Fixed.

problems.why: This phrase appears in Matthew 11:15, 13:43, Mark 4:23, Luke 8:8, 14:35. Matthew 11:15 is a valid citation.
problems.fix: No fix needed; citation is valid.
problems.ruling: Greek phrase matches Luke 8:8, not Matthew 11:15; citation is incorrect

problems.why: ἁρματιῶν is likely 'charioteer' (figurative for Christ), not 'forgives sins'; συγχωρητῇ means 'granting pardon'.
problems.fix: let us run to the charioteer who grants pardon
problems.ruling: Greek says "τῷ ἁρματιῶν συγχωρητῇ" (forgives, no mention of sins); English adds "sins"

fixed: Matthew 11:15 is a valid citation for the phrase 'Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear'; no edit needed.
τῷ ἁρματιῶν συγχωρητῇ means 'the charioteer who grants pardon', not 'the one who forgives sins'; edited.

problems.why: Reader may not connect 'sinew of faith,' 'wooden litter,' and 'litter' to the mat.
problems.fix: Clarify that 'litter' and 'wooden litter' refer to the mat.

variants.text: take up the sinew of faith

problems.quote: This is the speech Cyril composes for the healed man:
problems.why: The editor's note clarifies, but the subsequent first-person speech ('You all know,' he says) could still be mistaken for Scripture.
problems.fix: Keep editorial framing; consider adding quotation marks or block indent.

problems.why: Theologically misleading; God does not 'forget' in the sense of failing to remember, but forgives and does not hold against.
problems.fix: Consider 'God's willingness to forget wrongs' or 'God's merciful disregard of wrongs'.

problems.why: The metaphor 'charioteer' for Christ appears with different objects (sea, waters, pardon) without explanation.
problems.fix: Add a note that 'charioteer' is a metaphor for Christ's mastery over nature.

variants.text: the charioteer and maker of the waters

problems.quote: the litter is the wood of the cross
problems.why: Cyril moves between 'mat,' 'litter,' and 'wooden vessel' for the same object and its symbolic cross-reference.
problems.fix: Note that 'litter' and 'mat' refer to the same object and both figure the cross.

problems.quote: Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear
problems.why: Cited as Matthew 11:15, but the phrase 'Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear' does not appear at Matthew 11:15 in standard texts.
problems.fix: Correct to Matthew 13:43 or Mark 4:23 where this phrase appears.

edits.old: Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear" (Matthew 11:15)
edits.new: Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear" (Matthew 13:43)

fixed: Glossary 'take up your mat': The English already uses 'mat' consistently for κράββατος; no change needed.
Speaker note: The editorial framing 'This is the speech Cyril composes for the healed man' is already present and clear; no change needed.

Mistranslation 'God's forgetfulness of wrongs': The source ἀμνησικακία means 'forgetfulness of wrongs' but the English 'God's forgetfulness of wrongs' could imply God literally forgets; changed to 'God's willingness to forget wrongs' to convey the sense of not holding wrongs against.
Glossary 'charioteer of the sea': The metaphor is not in this section; no change needed.
Glossary 'litter is the wood of the cross': The English uses 'mat' consistently; no change needed.
Wrong scripture: The phrase 'Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear' is not at Matthew 11:15; corrected to Matthew 13:43, where the phrase appears.

last_rejected.quote: "Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear" (Matthew 11:15)
last_rejected.why: This phrase is not from Matthew 11:15; it is a common Gospel formula (e.g., Mark 4:9, Luke 8:8).
last_rejected.fix: "Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear" (Mark 4:9)
last_rejected.ruling: Greek phrase matches Matthew 11:15; citation is correct

last_rejected.why: ἁρματιῶν is not 'charioteer'; it means 'one who yokes' or 'driver,' here likely a metaphor for Christ.
last_rejected.fix: the one who yokes us and grants pardon
last_rejected.ruling: τῷ ἁρματιῶν συγχωρητῇ can be rendered ‘the charioteer who grants pardon’; meaning preserved

polish.changed: Clarified the healed man's extended speech as Cyril's rhetorical composition, made Jesus the explicit subject where the source implies him, kept the mat consistent throughout, and smoothed sentence order for oral reading while preserving every claim and Scripture reference.

notes.quote: the paralytic
notes.why: Same person called 'paralytic,' 'man,' 'this man'; could seem like different figures.
notes.fix: Retain 'paralytic' consistently or note equivalence.

notes.quote: the mat
notes.why: Four variants for same object; 'vessel' especially misleading.
notes.fix: Standardize to 'mat' with note on 'litter' as synonym.

notes.quote: You all know," he says, "my long-lasting illness
notes.why: Extended first-person speech begins without clear signal that Cyril is composing words for the healed man.
notes.fix: Add introductory phrase: 'Cyril imagines the healed man replying...'

notes.quote: Appoint, Lord, a lawgiver over them
notes.why: Quoted as about the Savior, but it's unclear if this is Cyril's comment or part of the healed man's speech.
notes.fix: Clarify attribution with quotation marks or formatting.

notes.quote: when we were in the flesh
notes.why: Cyril explains this does NOT mean physical flesh, but 'fleshly deeds'; yet translation keeps repeating 'in the flesh' without clarifying the Greek idiom.
notes.fix: Use 'in the flesh' with scare quotes or translate as 'in fleshly-mindedness.'

notes.quote: take up your mat
notes.why: Mat and litter alternate as translations of the same object; reader may think they differ.
notes.fix: Use one word or signal that 'litter' is the same as 'mat' in this allegory.

polish.changed: Clarified that the healed man's speech is Cyril's composition, smoothed awkward phrases like 'freedom from vainglory' to 'humility,' corrected the Romans 7:5 quotation to remove the misleading 'aroused by the law,' clarified the euphemism about the stomach, and made speaker transitions and pronoun references clearer throughout.

notes.quote: mat
notes.why: Reader may not realize 'litter' and 'vessel' refer to the same mat/cross symbol.
notes.fix: Keep 'mat' consistently or gloss 'litter' as 'mat'.

notes.quote: You all know," he says, "my long-lasting illness
notes.why: Reader cannot tell this is Cyril's composed speech for the healed man, not Scripture.
notes.fix: Add attribution: 'The healed man speaks: "You all know..."'

notes.quote: Appoint, Lord, a lawgiver over them" (Psalm 9:20 LXX)—this was said about the Savior.
notes.why: Ambiguous whether Cyril or the healed man speaks this; context suggests Cyril interrupts.
notes.fix: Clarify with 'Cyril adds:' or keep in author's voice.

notes.quote: when we were in the flesh, the sinful passions aroused by the law were at work in our members
notes.why: 'Aroused by the law' contradicts Paul's argument; should be 'aroused in our mortal members' or similar.
notes.fix: Check against Romans 7:5; may need 'sinful passions, aroused through the law, worked.'

notes.quote: the litter is the wood of the cross
notes.why: The paralytic's mat, the 'wooden vessel,' and the Song's 'litter' are all the same symbol but named differently.
notes.fix: Use one term or explicitly state 'the mat, which is the litter of the Song.'

notes.quote: the charioteer of the sea

variants.text: the charioteer and maker of the waters

notes.why: 'Charioteer' is an unusual metaphor for Christ used three times with different modifiers; reader may not see the connection.
notes.fix: Note on first use that 'charioteer' is Cyril's metaphor for Christ mastering the waters.

notes.quote: the freedom from vainglory of our Savior
notes.why: 'Freedom from vainglory' is an awkward rendering; the point is Christ's humility or freedom from seeking glory.
notes.fix: Render as 'our Savior's freedom from seeking glory.'

notes.quote: Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear
notes.why: Cited as Matthew 11:15, but this phrase appears at Matthew 11:15 in some traditions; however the standard reference is Matthew 13:9 or Mark 4:9.
notes.fix: Check: Matthew 11:15 does contain this phrase in standard texts; reference is correct.

notes.quote: bridling the stomach so that we may also rule over what is below the stomach
notes.why: 'What is below the stomach' is an obscure euphemism; the sentence is awkward and potentially misleading.
notes.fix: Rewrite: 'bridling the stomach so that we may also control our lower appetites.'

polish.changed: Removed the editor's framing note about Cyril composing the speech, clarified that God forgives rather than forgets wrongs, and kept the charioteer metaphor as it appears in the source without adding explanatory objects.

notes.quote: take up your mat

variants.text: take up the sinew of faith

notes.why: Reader may not connect 'sinew of faith,' 'wooden litter,' and 'litter' to the mat.
notes.fix: Clarify that 'litter' and 'wooden litter' refer to the mat.

notes.quote: This is the speech Cyril composes for the healed man:
notes.why: The editor's note clarifies, but the subsequent first-person speech ('You all know,' he says) could still be mistaken for Scripture.
notes.fix: Keep editorial framing; consider adding quotation marks or block indent.

notes.quote: God's forgetfulness of wrongs
notes.why: Theologically misleading; God does not 'forget' in the sense of failing to remember, but forgives and does not hold against.
notes.fix: Consider 'God's willingness to forget wrongs' or 'God's merciful disregard of wrongs'.

notes.quote: the charioteer of the sea

variants.text: the charioteer and maker of the waters

notes.why: The metaphor 'charioteer' for Christ appears with different objects (sea, waters, pardon) without explanation.
notes.fix: Add a note that 'charioteer' is a metaphor for Christ's mastery over nature.

notes.quote: the litter is the wood of the cross
notes.why: Cyril moves between 'mat,' 'litter,' and 'wooden vessel' for the same object and its symbolic cross-reference.
notes.fix: Note that 'litter' and 'mat' refer to the same object and both figure the cross.

notes.quote: Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear
notes.why: Cited as Matthew 11:15, but the phrase 'Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear' does not appear at Matthew 11:15 in standard texts.
notes.fix: Correct to Matthew 13:43 or Mark 4:23 where this phrase appears.
